statement: In 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had recently completed detoxification (one open-label feasibility study in the UK, all White British, with no comparison group), an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions that included two MDMA sessions was followed, 3 months after treatment, by self-reported drinking at least two WHO risk levels lower than at baseline in 9 of the 14 (64%; 95% CI 35% to 87%), which the authors' Bayesian analysis restates as a success rate of 55% to 63%; self-reported craving, a four-item sleep score and self-compassion also improved in the 13 or 14 with data, while quality of life did not change significantly after correction (11 with data). The trial registry places the drinking baseline before detoxification, the outcomes were self-reported by people who knew they had taken MDMA, the two-level endpoint was not a registered outcome, and the registered 6- and 9-month results are not in this report, so none of these changes can be attributed to MDMA. No randomized or otherwise controlled trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in alcohol use disorder was among the sources read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small UK study, 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had just been through detox had a talking-therapy course with two MDMA sessions. Three months later, 9 of the 14 reported drinking much less than at the start (which seems to mean before detox). There was no group without MDMA, and drinking was self-reported, so we cannot tell whether MDMA helped.
population: Adults aged 18 to 65 (registry) with a primary DSM-5 diagnosis of alcohol use disorder who had completed detoxification; excluded: psychotic, bipolar I or personality disorders, serious suicide risk, cardiovascular or severe liver disease, regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence, and antidepressants unless stopped
exposure: An eight-week recovery-based psychotherapy course of ten sessions, two of them with MDMA, with an overnight stay after each MDMA session
comparator: None: each participant's own baseline (for drinking, apparently drinking before detoxification, per the registry)
outcome: Reduction of at least two WHO drinking risk levels (Timeline Followback) 3 months after treatment; craving (PACS, OCDS), sleep, quality of life (SF-36), self-compassion and empathy at 3 months
magnitude: Two-level WHO risk reduction: 9 of 14 (proportion .64; binomial test against 50%, P = .423; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87); mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior (editors' check: posterior means 0.625 and 0.556). Three months vs baseline: PACS −5.50 (95% CI 0.5 to 13; n = 13); OCDS obsessive −5.00 (2.00 to 8.50) and compulsive −5.00 (1.00 to 9.00); four-item sleep score −2.00 (n = 14); Self-Compassion Scale +12.1 (9.09 to 14.4; n = 13); no SF-36 subscale significant after Bonferroni correction (n = 11). Within-group changes only.

evidence.locator: Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 9 of 14 reached a two-level reduction in WHO drinking risk at 3 months; binomial test against 50%: proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87; mean posterior 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with the sceptical Beta(1,3) prior.

evidence.locator: Results › Drinking behavior at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
evidence.extracted: At 3 months vs baseline (n = 13): PACS total difference 5.50 (95% CI .5 to 13), P = .031; OCDS obsessive 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006; OCDS compulsive 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

evidence.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Quality of life, Sleep and Self-compassion, 1st paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend
evidence.extracted: SF-36 (n = 11): no subscale significant after Bonferroni correction; four PSQI-derived sleep items (n = 14): difference 2.00, P = .041; Self-Compassion Scale (n = 13): +12.1 (95% CI 9.09 to 14.4), P < .001.

Fourteen participants with alcohol use disorder who had recently undergone detoxification completed the eight-week course of ten sessions, two with MDMA; 8 men and 6 women, mean age 48, all White British.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Single-group open-label phase 1 study, actual start 18 April 2018, first submitted 31 January 2019 (retrospective registration); drinking registered as change by Timeline Followback from pre-detoxification (screening) levels to session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months; no two-level WHO endpoint registered; questionnaires registered at 3, 6 and 9 months; no results posted.

The authors call the study an open-label trial with a small population, acknowledge possible Type I error inflation, call the findings hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of efficacy, and ask for randomized placebo-controlled trials that measure de-blinding and expectancy, and for long-term follow-up.

The authors compare the 55% to 63% success rate with 68% of patients reaching a two-level WHO risk reduction at the end of treatment in secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH: a comparison across studies, not within this one.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison group, pre-detoxification baseline, unblinded self-report, unregistered endpoint.

grade.reasoning: One single-arm open-label study of 14 people; for the question of effect it is non-randomized, so it starts low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical): no comparison group; a drinking baseline that the registry places before detoxification, so a fall after detoxification is expected whatever the treatment; self-reported outcomes from people who knew they had taken MDMA; unexplained missing questionnaire data; an unregistered endpoint, with the registered 6- and 9-month results unreported. Imprecision one level: 14 people, with a 95% interval from 35% to 87% for the endpoint. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to this population and time point; publication bias not assessable from one study. The relation is 'insufficient evidence': the design cannot show whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes drinking, and the statement only describes what was observed.

verification.flag_note: The original report of the same 14 participants (Sessa et al., 2021, J Psychopharmacol, doi 10.1177/0269881121991792) is not free and was not read; its safety and 9-month drinking data should be added before this claim is shown.
